t: Liberation theology interprets the Gospel through the lens of the oppressed, and its best-known phrase, the preferential option for the poor, describes an obligation of those who call themselves Christian first of all to care for the poor and vulnerable.

It drew heavily on Marxist social analysis, though it did not adopt Marxism wholesale, and the Vatican's Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, led by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, criticised it in the mid-1980s for excessive politicisation.

Its ideas spread beyond Latin America and beyond Catholicism, into black theology, Dalit theology, Palestinian liberation theology and Protestant thought, and Pope Francis later drew on liberationist ideas.
dyk: Hélder Câmara, the Brazilian archbishop, said: "When I give food to the poor, they call me a saint. When I ask why they are poor, they call me a communist."
ev: Liberation theologies are first discussed in Latin America, especially within Catholicism after the Second Vatican Council
Protestant advocates including C. René Padilla call for integral mission, emphasising evangelism and social responsibility
The Peruvian priest Gustavo Gutiérrez coins the term and writes A Theology of Liberation
Dalit theology emerges among the Dalit castes of the Indian subcontinent
The Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith admonishes certain forms of Latin American liberation theology for their reliance on Marxism

f.where: Latin America, above all within the Catholic Church in Peru, Brazil, El Salvador and Uruguay; related theologies in the United States, South Africa, among Palestinians, India, South Korea and Ireland
f.period: discussed in Latin America in the 1960s after the Second Vatican Council; term coined in 1971; Protestant calls for integral mission in the 1970s; height in the 1970s and 1980s; Vatican admonition in the mid-1980s; continuing influence since
f.figures: Gustavo Gutiérrez, who coined the term; Leonardo Boff; Jon Sobrino; Juan Luis Segundo; Frei Betto; Óscar Romero; Hélder Câmara, Brazilian archbishop; Protestant advocates Rubem Alves, José Míguez Bonino and C. René Padilla
f.outcome: grassroots ecclesial communities that mobilised for land reform, labour rights and democratic governance; criticism from Pope John Paul II and the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith; waning prominence after the 1980s, with continuing influence in theology, scholarship and social movements
